title: Dancing with the Stats Survival Analysis
text:
Dancing with the Stars (DWTS) is a reality competition show where 11-14 celebrities are each paired with a professional ballroom dancer. Every week, the pairs perform a dance (Cha-Cha, Tango, Waltz, Samba, Foxtrot, and so on), get scored by a panel of judges, and face a combination of judge scores and fan votes that decides who goes home. A season runs about 7-10 weeks, with one to three couples eliminated each week, until a handful of finalists remain in the last week to compete for the Mirrorball Trophy.



A DWTS season is the perfect set-up for a survival analysis. Everyone starts at the same time, people get eliminated (the event) along the way, and the contestants who make it to the finale never experience elimination (censored). That makes it a natural fit for survival analysis, which is built for exactly this kind of time-to-event data. This project started as our final project for STA 379 (Survival Analysis) at Wake Forest, and it asks two questions: which celebrity characteristics are related to how long a contestant lasts in a DWTS season, and how well can those characteristics predict who goes home?

title: Dancing with the Stats Survival Analysis
text:
Dancing with the Stars (DWTS) is a reality competition show where 11-14 celebrities are each paired with a professional ballroom dancer. Every week, the pairs perform a dance (Cha-Cha, Tango, Waltz, Samba, Foxtrot, and so on), get scored by a panel of judges, and face a combination of judge scores and fan votes that decides who goes home. A season runs about 7-10 weeks, with one to three couples eliminated each week, until a handful of finalists remain in the last week to compete for the Mirrorball Trophy.



A DWTS season is the perfect set-up for a survival analysis. Everyone starts at the same time, people get eliminated (the event) along the way, and the contestants who make it to the finale never experience elimination (censored). That makes it a natural fit for survival analysis, which is built for exactly this kind of time-to-event data. This project started as our final project for STA 379 (Survival Analysis) at Wake Forest, and it asks two questions: which celebrity characteristics are related to how long a contestant lasts in a DWTS season, and how well can those characteristics predict who goes home?

title: Dancing with the Stats Survival Analysis
text:
Behind the Scenes

Data Source
To answer these questions, we used a Dancing with the Stars dataset from Kaggle that includes our covariates of interest (sex, celebrity industry, week one average judge score, age) and the week they were eliminated. The dataset didn’t originally include celebrity sex, so we used Claude to add that column before analysis, and verified its accuracy.
We excluded Season 15, an all-star season of returning contestants, and Season 26, a shortened season made up entirely of athletes, which were both atypical seasons in term of celebrity makeup. That left us with a final sample of 371 contestants.


Survival Set Up
The trickiest part of the setup was deciding what “time” means. Seasons have different numbers of weeks, so being eliminated in week 5 means something very different in an 8-week season than in a 10-week one. Instead of raw weeks, we used the percent of the season completed at elimination as our time variable. Below, we define key criteria for the survival analysis setup.

Event: Elimination from competition
Time (perc_season): percent of season completed (season lengths varied)
Event indicator (Δ): Δ = 1 = eliminated (Contestants who were eliminated before the final week.) Δ = 0 = censored (Contestants who made it to the final week and placed - 1st,2nd,3rd,etc.)

This left us with an event rate of 78.9%.


Covariates
We looked at four covariates: two categorical (celebrity sex and celebrity industry) and two numeric (celebrity age during the season and their average judge score in week 1, which we used as a measure of baseline dance ability). Industry had a lot of small categories, so we collapsed it into Actor/Actress (n = 117), Athlete (n = 76), TV Personality (n = 59), Singer/Rapper (n = 57), and Other (n = 62), which lumped together everyone else.


Packages
The analysis relies on dplyr for data wrangling, survival for fitting Kaplan-Meier curves, log-rank tests, and Cox models, survminer for plotting survival curves, and knitr for tables. For the prediction piece, we used hdmetrics, which isn’t on CRAN and can be installed from GitHub:


Show the code
pak::pak("sarahlotspeich/hdmetrics/hdmetrics")

library(dplyr)
library(survival)
library(survminer)
library(knitr)
library(hdmetrics)

title: Dancing with the Stats Survival Analysis
text:
Analysis

Overall survival
To start, we fit a Kaplan-Meier curve for all contestants.


Show the code
km_overall <- survfit(Surv(perc_season, event) ~ 1, 
                      data = dwts_data, conf.type = "log-log")

ggsurvplot(km_overall, data = dwts_data,
           conf.int = TRUE, surv.median.line = "hv",
           xlab = "Proportion of Season Completed",
           ylab = "Survival Probability",
           palette = "purple", ggtheme = theme_bw())








Figure 1: Overall Kaplan-Meier curve for time to elimination. The dashed lines mark the median: half of contestants are eliminated by 70% of the way through the season.



Of our 371 contestants, 281 were eliminated and the rest made it to the finale. As Figure 1 shows, the curve drops steadily across the season, which makes sense: with eliminations every week, everyone’s risk of going home accumulates over time. The median survival time was 0.70 (95% CI: 0.67 to 0.80), meaning that by 70% of the way through a season, half the contestants have been sent home.


Categorical Covariates: Does sex or industry matter?
Next, we compared survival across groups using Kaplan-Meier curves and log-rank tests. For celebrity sex, the curves for men and women are practically on top of each other (Figure 2).


Show the code
fit_sex <- survfit(Surv(perc_season, event) ~ celebrity_sex, 
                   data = dwts_data, conf.type = "plain")

logrank_sex <- survdiff(Surv(perc_season, event) ~ celebrity_sex, 
                        data = dwts_data, rho = 0)








Figure 2: Kaplan-Meier curves for time to elimination by celebrity sex, with 95% confidence bands.



Industry was more interesting to look at. In Figure 3, the “Other” category drops off noticeably earlier than everyone else, losing about a quarter of its contestants within the first 20% of the season. Actors, athletes, singers, and TV personalities all track pretty closely together. This tracks with our hypothesis that contestants who have experience performing in the public eye, which are all characteristics actors, athletes, singers and TV personalities share, may last longer in the DWTS season.


Show the code
fit_industry <- survfit(Surv(perc_season, event) ~ celebrity_industry, 
                        data = dwts_data, conf.type = "plain")

logrank_industry <- survdiff(Surv(perc_season, event) ~ celebrity_industry, 
                             data = dwts_data, rho = 0)








Figure 3: Kaplan-Meier curves for time to elimination by celebrity industry.



However, neither difference held up statistically. The log-rank tests failed to reject the null hypothesis for both covariates, so we can’t conclude that sex or industry is related to time to elimination.

Log-rank test results for the categorical covariates.

Numeric Covariates: Does age and week 1 scores matter?
For our numeric covariates, we fit a separate Cox proportional hazards model for each one and checked the proportional hazards assumption with cox.zph().


Show the code
cox_age   <- coxph(Surv(perc_season, event) ~ celebrity_age_during_season, 
                   data = dwts_data)
cox_score <- coxph(Surv(perc_season, event) ~ week1_avg_judge_score, 
                   data = dwts_data)

cox.zph(cox_age)
cox.zph(cox_score)


Both turned out to be strong predictors (p < 0.001 for each).

Cox proportional hazards model results for the numeric covariates.


Covariate

(0.027, 0.043)

(-0.579, -0.389)

Age: Each additional year of age increases the hazard of elimination by about 3.6%. That adds up quickly. Comparing a 59-year-old contestant to a 25-year-old one, the model puts the older contestant’s hazard of elimination at roughly 3.3 times higher.
Week 1 score: Each additional point in a contestant’s week 1 average judge score multiplies their hazard of elimination by about 0.62. In plain terms, a strong first week is a very good sign.
The proportional hazards check told a more nuanced story. Age passed comfortably (p = 0.79), meaning its effect is roughly constant across the whole season. Week 1 score did not (p = 0.005), meaning its effect changes over time. Our hunch is that a great first performance matters a lot early on but fades as the season goes on and contestants improve (or don’t).


Side Quest: Can we predict who goes home?
Finally, we fit a Cox model with all four covariates and asked how well it could tell contestants apart over the course of a season. We used km_auroc() from hdmetrics to estimate the time-dependent area under the ROC curve (AUC) at 25%, 50%, and 75% of the way through the season.


Show the code
cox_full <- coxph(Surv(perc_season, event) ~ week1_avg_judge_score +
                    celebrity_age_during_season + celebrity_sex + 
                    celebrity_industry,
                  data = dwts_data)

dwts_data$betaZ <- cox_full$linear.predictors

km_auroc(evaluate_at = c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75),
         time = "perc_season", event = "event",
         log_risk = "betaZ", data = dwts_data)


An AUC of 1 means perfect discrimination and 0.5 is a coin flip. If you pick two contestants at a given point in the season, one who has already been eliminated and one who hasn’t, the AUC is the probability that the model assigned the higher risk to the one who went home.

Time-dependent AUC for the full Cox model.

The model does a decent job early on but drifts toward a coin flip as the season goes on. That lines up with the proportional hazards result above: almost all of our covariates are measured at the start of the season, and the biggest predictor, the week 1 score, says less and less about who survives as the weeks go by.

title: Dancing with the Stats Survival Analysis
text:
Conclusion
So who survives the ballroom? Based on our analysis, it’s not about whether you’re a man or a woman or what made you famous. It’s about being younger and walking in with some baseline dance ability. Age and week 1 score were both strong predictors of how long a celebrity lasts, while sex and industry showed no significant relationship with elimination.One thing we wish we had access to with the Kaggle dataset was some measure of a contestants popularity with America, like average votes across their time on the season. Even though judges score are important in remaining on the season, fan base is a very important factor, too (example: king Guillermo!!!!). This project was an engaging way to apply our coursework from our survival course with Dr. Sarah Lotspiech in a fun and meaningful way. We are excited to see who will bring home this season’s mirrorball (we’re rooting for Ezra or Maura!!!).

title: Every Man’s Causal Inference
text:
Context, Please

A little over ten years ago, I and two colleagues, Jeff Leek and Brian Caffo, developed this massive open online course (MOOC) on data science. It was one of the first ones and it was hugely popular, to our surprise. At some point, I think it was Brian who said we should write a textbook for each of these classes, so we did a crash program of writing textbooks for each of the courses.

Then it came down to how do we distribute the books? We found a self-publishing platform called Leanpub and we put it on there. One of the interesting things about Leanpup was that it allowed people to set their own price. You could set it between zero and nine hundred and ninety-nine dollars or something like that. We had a suggested price, and most people, unsurprisingly, set it to zero, but some people paid.

title: Every Man’s Causal Inference
text:
Behind the Scenes

The publisher platform gives you data on all of your sales. You can click a button and you get this CSV file of every sale that occurs.

title: Every Man’s Causal Inference
text:
Analysis

The pre-post

We had so many people enrolled in this MOOC, and it was a synchronous program at the time, so everyone enrolled the first of the month. We send this email out on the second of the month, and the sales just skyrocketed on the third day of the month. It didn’t originally occur to us that because there are a hundred thousand people enrolled in this class, even if ten percent of them decided to buy the book, it was the most number of sales that we’ve ever had in our entire lives. Now okay, most of them were for zero dollars. It wasn’t like everyone was paying money. But that was my lesson number one in causal inference, a pre-post test.



The ten percent law

It was interesting to see who paid and who didn’t. The distribution is bimodal. There is one mode at zero, and then at the suggested price, and then a couple of blips a little bit higher. And it seemed across the board, of all the books that we had available, ten percent seemed pretty universal, which I think is interesting. Granted, across the courses, the people are the same for the most part. But I had a podcast, and we had a Patreon and based on the rough numbers that we got from the podcast provider, it also was around ten percent of people who paid for the Patreon. So anyway, ten percent. That’s the universal law.

title: Every Man’s Causal Inference
text:
Conclusions

I think side projects in general, especially in academia, are good just to keep yourself busy. In academia people often talk about being innovative. There’s a lot of talk of innovation, but to me, that’s the nature of what all these side projects are. Some of them turn into something and it’s like, that person’s so innovative. Well, yeah, but up until a minute ago, they were just wasting time. That’s why side projects are important, because you’re wasting time up until the point where it’s ingenious.

title: Election Data Web Scraping
text:
On even numbered years, I spend a lot of my free time volunteering with downballot voter turnout initiatives. Over the years, I’ve worked across 10+ states – each with their unique datasets and data debacles. While there are some standard vendors and APIs, much of the final voter turnout data is highly bespoke. Every state – even county – in the country can come up with it’s own publishing format (federalism, eh?) leading to unique data collection challenges.
Trying to scrape and wrangle this data has proven a fun survey on the wide breadth of automated data collection tools. Even moreso, it’s cause to reflect on how different data formats cater to the needs of different audiences and how design choices as data publishers can be more or less constructive to different audiences.
I also failed to give a good answer when asked on the pod how to help turnout voters because – hey, I’m just the data person. But realistically the most important thing you can do is tell people in your life to vote, ask them their plan, offer them a ride. What the data does often imply is that you should never underestimate how many non-voters (although behavior is admittedly highly correlated) you probably know. Help them know their voice matters.

title: Election Data Web Scraping
text:
Behind the Scenes
The data can come from any number of state and county websites. Packages vary based on the setup, including:

direct file download with requests
basic static web scraping with BeautifulSoup
dynamic web scraping with Playwright
headless browser automation with Playwright
screenshotting and image parsing with tesseract

Examples of different pipelines and patterns can be found in:

Goin’ to Carolina on my Drive – blog from 2022. Could be much further optimized now with advanced in polars and duckdb. CSV sniffing, for one, has improved a lot
A Tale of Six States – blog from 2021. Some states have changes formats since so are outdated
GitHub Repo – update of the 6 states from 2024. Less out of date?

I’ve been tracking my more recent travails updating pre-existing data pipelines on Bluesky.

title: Election Data Web Scraping
text:
Analysis
I think a lot of people know about basic web scraping already, so here, I will demonstrate my favorite and lesser used pattern: headless browser automation. While it has a crazy name, the simple idea is to ask your computer to do very human steps of navigating a browser: looking, finding, clicking, selecting, waiting, refreshing, etc. This is easily down with the python package Playwright.
To navigate and download files from the [Texas Secretary of State], I wanted to follow the steps illustrated below:

This is accomplished by this relatively minial script. The real trick is using your browser’s developer tools to identify what fields you want to target.


Show the code
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright
import datetime

def retrieve_date(date, page):

  # navigate to date-specific page 
  target_date = datetime.datetime.strptime(date, '%Y%m%d')
  target_date_str = target_date.strftime('%Y-%m-%d 00:00:00.0')
  target_file = 'tx-' + target_date.strftime('%Y%m%d') + '.csv'
  
  # pick election
  page.goto('https://earlyvoting.texas-election.com/Elections/getElectionDetails.do')
  page.select_option('#idElection', label = "2020 NOVEMBER 3RD GENERAL ELECTION")
  page.click('#electionsInfoForm button')
  page.wait_for_selector('#selectedDate')
  
  # pick day
  page.select_option('#selectedDate', value = target_date_str)
  page.click('#electionsInfoForm button:nth-child(2)')
  page.wait_for_selector('"Generate Statewide Report"')

  # download report  
  with page.expect_download() as download_info:
    page.click('"Generate Statewide Report"')
  download = download_info.value
  download.save_as(f'data/{target_file}')

with sync_playwright() as p:

  browser = p.firefox.launch()
  # want to see it in action? Switch to firefox.launch(headless=False, slow_mo=50)
  context = browser.new_context(accept_downloads = True)
  page = context.new_page()
  
  dates = ['20201020','20201021','20201022']
  for d in dates:
    retrieve_date(d, page)

  # cleanup
  page.close()
  context.close()
  browser.close()


I personally am much more interested in collecting this data for mercenary operational purposes than for analysis, so I don’t have pretty plots and charts to share. However, I will mention that the NC election data is a special type of amazing with rich history and metadata as required by state law. It’s become one of my favorite datasets to do a quick test of different modeling ideas (my personal penguins). If anyone wants it to play with or use for a class, please feel free to reach out and I would be happy to share.

title: The Speed of Justice, According to Law & Order
text:
Context, Please
Law & Order is a TV show that has been on the air since 1990. (It originally aired from 1990 to 2010, then was revived in 2022.) Its basic formula is summarized neatly by the opening narration, which is followed by a famous DUN-DUN sound: “In the criminal justice system, the people are represented by two separate, yet equally important, groups: the police, who investigate crime; and the district attorneys, who prosecute the offenders. These are their stories.”
As an avid watcher of the show and its spinoffs, especially Law & Order: Special Victims Unit, I have long wondered: How long does it actually take in Law & Order land for the criminal justice system to work, compared with how long it takes in reality?
I started a newsletter called Wrong Number with two friends, Caitlin Gilbert and John Harden, to nerd out on data fixations like this one! More details about how I got the data and did the analysis are in my first post, which this one is adapted from. While you’re there, check out Caitlin’s post about theme park accidents and John’s about the kinds of trees that are found in each city.

title: The Speed of Justice, According to Law & Order
text:
Behind the Scenes
Law & Order has episode scene cards that demarcate major scene changes. A scene card has the date and address where the scene is supposed to be taking place. The intrepid fans on the show’s Fandom Wiki have diligently jotted down the contents of the episode scene cards for a vast majority of episodes. I compiled the available episode scene card data from every episode of Law & Order (this goes through Season 25, Episode 12).
I calculated the time between the first scene card and the final scene card to determine the length of time elapsed over the course of the episode.
Separately, I cross-referenced my information using a spreadsheet I came across on The Comic Board discussion forum: A fan had used the scene cards as guideposts, but also looked at the outfits the characters were wearing from scene to scene to determine whether that scene took place the same day as the preceding one, as well as using dialogue clues.

title: The Speed of Justice, According to Law & Order
text:
Analysis
Here’s a histogram showing the distribution of the time elapsed in each episode. The average Law & Order episode takes place over the course of about 68 days. How does that compare with reality?



A timeline of cases in Law & Order


According to a 2024 report commissioned by the New York City Comptroller: “Since 2019, the average time to process a murder case has risen by 37%, by an average of 221 days, from just over nineteen months to almost 27 months.” 27 months = 821 days.
So, justice in Law & Order land happens about 13 times as fast as it does in reality. If anything, this is an underestimate of how quickly justice is served on the show vs. in real life, because the report measures the amount of time from the initial arrest to the resolution of the trial. An episode of L&O, by contrast, typically begins when the crime is committed. So, if anything, Law & Order should take longer than it does in reality, because the police take time to investigate the crime and identify the suspect.
I also made a Gantt chart to display the timeline of cases, to see cases that are effectively overlapping — e.g., detectives closing one case while in the midst of another. Here it is for L&O season 1, organized by episode air date.



A Gantt chart of cases in Law & Order season 1


Interestingly, the same chart for season 24 of Law & Order: Special Victims Unit shows cases that do not overlap at all and that take much less time than the ones in Law & Order season 1: an average of just 5.3 days. Why is this the case? Sex crimes, I would imagine, take even longer to investigate and prosecute in real life than murder or other kinds of felonies, if they even make it to trial. It could be that the writers’ rooms for these shows have gotten more self-aware about the dates they put on the episode scene cards, and there is some desire to reduce overlapping dates within a season (though, in my opinion, having overlapping dates would be more true to reality, not less).



A Gantt chart of cases in Law & Order: SVU season 24


You can find more analyses as well as the code I used to make these plots in my newsletter post!

title: The Speed of Justice, According to Law & Order
text:
Conclusion
In the fictional universe of Law & Order, justice is served swiftly and effectively, more so than in the real-life statistics on the criminal justice system.

title: The Speed of Justice, According to Law & Order
text:
Sidenotes
I am not a legal expert, and I could be off in my collection of the data, or my interpretation of the stats. If you have additional thoughts on this, please get in touch! You can email my newsletter at wrongnumbernewsletter @ gmail.com.
And finally, this summer (after the airing of the podcast episode) I went to see Mariska Hargitay, aka SVU Captain Olivia Benson in Every Brilliant Thing on Broadway. I was lucky enough to catch her last show, which also featured her husband, Peter Hermann (aka the recurring defense attorney Trevor Langan). Sadly I did not share the results of my analysis with them, but they were nice enough to sign my Playbill.



Every Brilliant Thing Playbill

title: Romance by the Numbers: First Sparks Across Tropes
text:
Context, Please!
Romance novels (in)famously guarantee happily ever afters (HEAs) and follow one of a few pathways (tropes) to get there. (See a nice overview of common tropes from Shondaland here.) On our first episode, we discussed Sarah’s recent side project using data to investigate whether different tropes speed up or slow down the couple getting together, even if all books are going to end with that HEA.

title: Romance by the Numbers: First Sparks Across Tropes
text:
Behind the Scenes
Sarah collected a sample of romance novels from the last 10 years that became popular in the U.S., recording the following key variables:

Main_Trope: the primary trope employed in the novel,
Page: the page on which the couple’s first kiss,
Total: the total number of pages in the novel (used to normalize across books of different lengths), and
Percent: the percent of the way through the book when the couple first kisses (calculated as Page/Total).

These data are publicly available! You can read them in and run the code below to replicate her analyses.


Show the code
# Load packages 
library(googlesheets4) ## for reading data directly from Google Sheets 
library(dplyr) ## for data manipulation
library(survival) ## for Kaplan-Meier estimator
library(survminer) ## for pretty survival curves 
library(ggplot2) ## for other data visualization
library(stringr) ## for cleaning string fields (tropes)

# Read the data
rom_dat = read_sheet("https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/10HZevTEd4CWjqIcVMbED2nkpmnXDV6NVxCKenCsUqv0/edit?usp=sharing") |> 
  mutate(Main_Trope = toupper(Main_Trope)) ## clean up text (make tropes all upper case)


There are a lot of different tropes, and this sample captured 13 unique ones. However, a few of them were fairly uncommon, so the tropes were regrouped with others that were thematically similar (with the help of ChatGPT).


Show the code
# Counts of books per original tropes 
table(rom_dat$Main_Trope) 



             BROTHER'S BEST FRIEND                  CELEBRITY ROMANCE 
                                 4                                  2 
                       FAKE DATING                   FORCED PROXIMITY 
                                 4                                  2 
                 FRIENDS-TO-LOVERS                    GRUMPY/SUNSHINE 
                                 5                                  9 
                        INSTA-LOVE                    LOVE AFTER LOSS 
                                 1                                  2 
               NO STRINGS ATTACHED RIVALS-TO-LOVERS/ENEMIES-TO-LOVERS 
                                 1                                  8 
             SECOND CHANCE ROMANCE                         SINGLE DAD 
                                 8                                  1 
                SURPRISE PREGNANCY 
                                 1 


Show the code
# Create trope groupings (collapse less-frequent tropes)
rom_dat = rom_dat |> 
  mutate(
    Main_Trope_Grouped = case_when(
      Main_Trope %in% c("FAKE DATING", "FORCED PROXIMITY", "SURPRISE PREGNANCY", "NO STRINGS ATTACHED") ~ "CONTRIVED/SITUATIONAL SETUP",
      Main_Trope %in% c("BROTHER'S BEST FRIEND", "CELEBRITY ROMANCE", "SINGLE DAD") ~ "POWER/STATUS/TABOO",
      .default = Main_Trope
    ), 
    Kissed = 1 ## Have to define an event indicator to fit Kaplan-Meier, but all are events 
  ) |> 
  filter(!(Main_Trope_Grouped %in% c("LOVE AFTER LOSS", "INSTA-LOVE"))) ## Exclude two uncommon tropes that couldn't naturally be grouped (loses 3 books)

# Counts of books per grouped tropes 
table(rom_dat$Main_Trope_Grouped) 



       CONTRIVED/SITUATIONAL SETUP                  FRIENDS-TO-LOVERS 
                                 8                                  5 
                   GRUMPY/SUNSHINE                 POWER/STATUS/TABOO 
                                 9                                  7 
RIVALS-TO-LOVERS/ENEMIES-TO-LOVERS              SECOND CHANCE ROMANCE 
                                 8                                  8 


After re-grouping, there were 6 unique values instead, with at least 5 books each.

title: Romance by the Numbers: First Sparks Across Tropes
section: Primary Analysis: Proportion of the Way Through the Book
text:
Primary Analysis: Proportion of the Way Through the Book
Kaplan-Meier curves can be used to compare how quickly book couples first kiss (a measure of their romantic pacing). The original analysis used Percent as the measure of “how quickly” the event occurred, so that we could compare pacing across shorter/longer books by standardizing them to be on the same relative scale.

Overall (All Tropes Together)


Show the code
# Fit Kaplan-Meier 
fit_overall = survfit(formula = Surv(time = Percent, event = Kissed) ~ 1, 
                      data = rom_dat)

# Plot overall Kaplan-Meier curve 
rom_cols <- c("#E63946", "#F1A7A7", "#A26769", "#6D2E46", "#CDB4DB",  "#D96C75") ### Define pretty color palette 
plot_overall = ggsurvplot(
  fit = fit_overall, 
  ### Customize the look of the plot 
  palette = rom_cols, 
  ggtheme = theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#F5E6E8", color = NA),  
    plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "#F5E6E8", color = NA),
    panel.grid = element_line(color = "#E3D3D6"),

title: The Work Is Mysterious and Important: Severance Data
text:
Context, Please
I am a huge fan of the show Severance. As I mention in the episode, I just love the amazing attention to detail throughout, it is such a fun show to watch and rewatch as a fan! I started collecting data while watching the show during its first season which resulted in an R package, mdr, as well as an elaborate fan site where I host lots of silly little analyses.

For today, I am going to walk through an in depth analysis on whether Seth Milchick actually uses “too many big words” as he was told during a performance review in Season 2.

The Art of Web Scraping Art
text: There is an artist I follow on TikTok, Weston Lambert, and I really liked his work. He has hundreds of thousands of followers on TikTok and Instagram, so as soon as he drops anything, it gets sold immediately. I got sick of seeing his post on social media, going to the website and seeing it was already sold out, so I decided I would write a scraper that would scrape his website every fifteen minutes and then message me if anything went on sale. And that eventually worked. That is how I got this piece.

The Marshmallow Test (Not That One)
text:
Context, Please
No debate in Israel is quite as heated as the one over the differences between white and pink marshmallows.
While some argue that white marshmallows taste the best, others sneer and laugh at that notion – of course the pink marshmallows are far superior! And yet, there is a third group, equally mocked by the white- and pink-lovers: those that claim no difference between the two colors at all!
Sounds like an empirical question to me! Let’s go answer it!

Is there a perceptible difference between white and pink marshmallows?

title: The Marshmallow Test (Not That One)
text:
Behind the Scenes
24 unassuming undergrad students in the Statistics and Data Analysis program at Ben-Gurion University and graduate students from the Psychology Department at Ben-Gurion University and the Psychology School at Tel Aviv University volunteered to eat some marshmallows. (Two additional data points were collected from me and my wife, Naama.)
The experiment had two parts: the triangle test and the identification test – a modern take on the lady tasting tea experiment.
In the triangle test, 3 marshmallows were placed in front of blindfolded participants: two were of the same color, and one was of a different color, with the order and colors randomly determined. Students were instructed to try and guess which was the odd-one-out. They were free to eat, taste, nibble, smell and do whatever they wanted.
After completing the triangle test, they were handed a fourth marshmallow (still blindfolded) for the identification test. The color of this marshmallow was also randomly determined.

title: The Marshmallow Test (Not That One)
text:
Analysis
The analysis uses the amazing brms package, the superb marginaleffects package for post-estimation processing, and the glorious ggdist for visualizing posterior distributions and uncertainty.

The Triangle Test
For the triangle test, a simple Bayesian logistic regression analysis was used to predict the probability of correctly identifying the odd-one-out. If there is a noticeable difference, we would expect this probability to be higher than chance - in this case 1/3. The color of the odd-one-out was also included to explore the possibility that it is easier/harder to detect an odd pink marshmallow than an odd white marshmallow.
So, Can people correctly identify the odd-colored marshmallow in a blind taste test?
It seems like people can - performing above chance (1/3), with a 90% HDI [0.36, 0.65], pd=97.35%! However, they seem to be better at doing this when the odd one out is pink than when it’s white…



The Identification Test
An additional Bayesian binomial model with a probit link was used, predicting participants’ responses from the actual color of the marshmallow. It can be shown that such a model can be used to estimate the Signal Detection Theory parameters, with the slope for the indicator variable being equal to \(d'\) and the intercept (\(\times -1\)) being equal to the criterion \(c\).
So can people reliably identify the pink marshmallow from the white marshmallow?
Using Signal Detection Theory (SDT), discriminability is captured by d-prime, and is conceptualized as the distance of the distribution of perceptual evidence for the pink marshmallow (Signal+Noise) from the distribution of perceptual evidence for the white marshmallow (Noise fixed at \(N(0, 1)\)). Here there was an 82.33% posterior probability that discriminability is greater than 0, but there was also a posterior probability of 27.5% that discriminability is less than 0.15… So pretty inconclusive.
But a true Bayesian embraces uncertainty!



Addendum
Following the recording of the episode, I received an official response from a food scientist on behalf of the marshmallow company:

There are no differences in the ingredients besides the colors, and the pink marshmallow contains strawberry extract.


The data and code behind this post can be found here.

title: Mixed Effects, Mixed Signals: Love Island Kissing Scores
text:
Love Island is a television show that started in the UK and now also has versions in the US and in Malta. Across all versions of the show, the basic premise is that 10-12 extremely hot people (5-6 men and 5-6 women) get put into a villa, where their goal is to form couples. Throughout each season, they go through various challenges and games, and then every week or so, the producers force them to “recouple” and dump some people from the villa. As people leave the villa, more hot people are brought in to mix up the existing couples, who are referred to as “bombshells”. At the end of the season, which lasts for 6-8 weeks, the public votes one of the lasting couples as the winner.



One infamous challenge on Love Island is the Kissing Challenge (also called Kissing Booth), which has been used on multiple seasons of every iteration of the show. In this challenge, either all of the men or all of the women (the Kissees) line up in blindfolds and headphones. The other gender (the Kissers) goes down the line one by one, kissing all of the Kissees, who subsequently score them out of 10. The contestants (or more likely, the producers helping execute the challenge) then tally up all the scores, and the Kisser with the highest score is crowned the winner. The only prize is bragging rights. On most seasons, the Kissing Challenge is only run in one direction (i.e., only the men or only the women get to be the Kissers), but on two seasons of Love Island USA, the contestants switch after completing one round, so that ultimately, there is a winning man and a winning woman. In this case, we also get scores for each woman kissing each man, as well as for each man kissing each woman.

title: Mixed Effects, Mixed Signals: Love Island Kissing Scores
text:
Behind the Scenes

Data source
Luckily, there are incredible people contributing to the Love Island ITV Wiki, who have already gone through the trouble of entering all of the data from the Kissing Challenge, so I could pretty easily compile it from each respective season of the challenge. Because only seasons USA 4 and 6 had truly reciprocal data, I ultimately only ended up using data from those seasons.


Setting up the data
To set up the data, I created a long version of the wiki data, so that each row represented one kiss interaction, with variables for the Season, the Kissee, their gender, the Kisser, the score they received, and a manually coded variable of whether those two individuals were ever in a couple throughout that season. I also created various dummy and contrast codes, and transformed group and individual IDs as needed to prepare for analyses, following pretty similar processes to Kluger et al. (2025).

title: Mixed Effects, Mixed Signals: Love Island Kissing Scores
text:
Analysis

What is the social relations model?
To explore this data, I used the social relations model, which conceptualizes dyadic interaction measures as containing actor, partner, relationship, and error variances and partitions these. In this case, dyadic simply refers to the fact that two people are involved in the interaction. Applied to this data, the actor effect describes the variance explained by systematic differences between Kissees. The partner effect describes the variance explained by systematic differences between the Kissers. The relationship effect would describe the “special spark” between certain individuals, but because there weren’t repeated measures taken (i.e., each Kisser only kissed each Kissee once), it isn’t possible to separate this effect from the error term. There are several ways to estimate social relations model parameters, which partially depend on how we treat the design of this “experiment”:
The first way I analyzed the data was to treat it as a round robin event, where individuals were simply cycling through each other giving kisses and ratings. This approach assumes there is no impact of gender or of which season the data is coming from. The advantage to this is that I could use the TripleR package (Schönbrodt et al., 2012), which uses the method of moments to estimate all the variances as well as covariances between actor and partner effects.


Show the code
RR1 <- RR(kiss_score~actorID*partnerID, data=li_ab_data, na.rm=TRUE)


Both partner and actor effects were significant. 21% of the variance in scores is driven by the Kisser, and only 6% of the variance in scores is driven by the Kissee. 73.2% of the variance in scores is explained by the combination of relationship effect and error.

Despite being able to analyze the data as a pure round robin, it’s more appropriate to characterize these interactions as an asymmetric block design, which refers to dyadic interactions where individuals fall into two groups (in this case, men and women). In an asymmetric block design, individuals interact only with those who are not in their in-group (in this case, men only kissing women, and women only kissing men). Kluger et al. (2025) provide an excellent tutorial on completing analyses on this type of data, essentially using a mixed-effects model where actor and partner exist as random effects, and fixed effects like gender, season, and couple status can be included as needed.


Show the code
mod <- glmmTMB(kiss_score ~1+mwVwm*ever_couple+gID+
                us(0+mw+wm|gID:mID)
                +us(0+wm+mw|gID:wID)
                +us(0+mw+wm|gID:mID:wID), 
                data=li_ab_data, 
                family=gaussian(link="identity"),
                dispformula=~0,
                REML=TRUE,
                verbose=FALSE,
                na.action=na.omit,
                control=glmmTMBControl(
                  optimizer=optim,
                  optArgs = list(method="BFGS"),
                  parallel = parallel::detectCores()))


There was no significant effect of men vs women being the Kisser (or Kissee), nor was there a significant effect of season, suggesting that men and women across seasons all rate kisses similarly on average. For men, the effect of partner (Kisser) accounted for 28% of the variance, and for women, this effect accounted for 31%. In this model, for both genders, the Kissee accounted for less than 1% of the variance. Results were broadly similar when I included couple status as a fixed effect, with the addition that being in a couple was associated with scoring approximately 0.75 points higher. Though there wasn’t a significant interaction between gender and couple status, the visual below of this fixed effect hints that women may be more impacted by couple status than men are.

I also played around with widening the data so that each row corresponded to a dyad (one man and one woman), with scores for both the instance when the man was the Kisser and when the woman was the Kisser. This let me play around with the extent to which scores were related to each other via correlation, which is conceptually similar to the concept of dyadic reciprocity in the social relations model. This can also be estimated using Kluger et al. (2025)’s approach, but it was easier to visualize by manipulating the data, so I did it anyway! Across models and a simple correlation, men and women’s scores were moderately correlated.
As a side side project, I decided it was critical to plot this wider data with emojis instead of standard data plots. This was surprisingly easy using the emoGG package, and allowed me to create this incredibly on-theme.

Using a similar plot, we can also see that couples overall tended to score each other higher. Unfortunately, I couldn’t figure out how to make create a plot with different emojis as the couple status indicators at this time, so we return to standard color indicators.

title: Mixed Effects, Mixed Signals: Love Island Kissing Scores
text:
Conclusion
It seems like despite all the messiness that comes with Love Island, the Kissing Challenge is actually relatively good at measuring what it purports to measure: the kissing ability of the Kisser! Another way to think about the significant partner effects is that the Kisser is deciding to send a certain message to the Kissee, and the results show that the Kissees’ scores reflect the variety of those messages. These results also suggest that, indeed, people who are in couples with each other tend to enjoy kissing each other more. There are tons of other ways one could analyze this data, and even more if the producers would find ways to get us more truly reciprocal data!
